title: Medieval and Modern History of Bihar — Statehood and the Freedom Struggle

blocks.content: Medieval and Modern History of Bihar — Statehood and the Freedom Struggle

Covers Bihar's medieval interlude through Sher Shah Suri, colonial administrative history, and its outsized role in India's freedom movement — culminating in Bihar becoming the first Indian province carved out of a Presidency along linguistic lines.

The medieval period saw Bihar largely governed as part of larger empires centred elsewhere — the Delhi Sultanate and later the Mughal Empire — though it produced one figure of genuinely first-rank importance in Indian history: Sher Shah Suri, who briefly interrupted Mughal rule under Humayun to establish the short-lived but administratively influential Suri Empire (1540–1545 CE). Born in Sasaram (in present-day Bihar), Sher Shah is remembered for major administrative reforms — including a revenue settlement system that influenced later Mughal administration — and for constructing the Grand Trunk Road, one of the oldest and longest major roads in South Asia, alongside his own mausoleum at Sasaram, widely regarded as an outstanding example of pre-Mughal Indo-Islamic architecture.

Under British colonial rule, the territory that is now Bihar was for a long period administered as part of the Bengal Presidency, with Patna functioning as a provincial centre rather than a capital in its own right. This changed in 1912, when Bihar and Orissa were separated from the Bengal Presidency to form a new province — Bihar and Orissa Province — making 1912 a landmark date in the state's administrative history. Orissa was subsequently separated as its own distinct province in 1936, after which the province was simply known as Bihar; this 1936 separation is frequently confused with the 1912 event in casual accounts, but the two are distinct and both are independently testable dates.

Bihar's contribution to India's freedom struggle was substantial and is anchored by one particularly celebrated episode: the Champaran Satyagraha of 1917, widely regarded as Mahatma Gandhi's first major civil disobedience campaign on Indian soil (following his earlier experience in South Africa). Responding to the grievances of indigo cultivators in the Champaran district who were being forced under the exploitative 'Tinkathia' system to grow indigo on a fixed portion of their land, Gandhi's intervention — supported by figures including Rajendra Prasad, who would later become independent India's first President — marked both a significant local victory for the cultivators and a formative moment in Gandhi's development of Satyagraha as a national political method. Bihar also saw substantial participation in subsequent movements, including the Non-Cooperation Movement, Civil Disobedience Movement, and Quit India Movement of 1942, during which Patna's Secretariat became the site of a notably significant and violently suppressed protest.
Sher Shah Suri and the Suri Empire

items: Sher Shah Suri, born Farid Khan in Sasaram, rose from a regional Bihar-based noble to briefly defeat the Mughal emperor Humayun and establish the Suri Empire (1540–1545 CE), ruling from Delhi but with deep roots in Bihar.

His administrative reforms included a systematic land revenue settlement, a reorganized currency system (including the introduction of the silver rupee, whose basic denomination influenced currency naming conventions for centuries afterward), and an efficient postal/communication (dak) system.

The Grand Trunk Road, significantly developed and extended under Sher Shah, remains one of the most historically significant transport arteries of South Asia, connecting the eastern and western parts of the subcontinent.
Sher Shah's mausoleum at Sasaram, built in the middle of an artificial lake, is widely regarded as one of the finest examples of pre-Mughal Indo-Islamic architecture in India.
For much of British colonial rule, the Bihar region was administered as part of the Bengal Presidency, without its own separate provincial identity.

In 1912, Bihar and Orissa were separated from the Bengal Presidency to form the new Bihar and Orissa Province — a landmark reorganization along more linguistically/regionally coherent lines, with Patna as its capital.

In 1936, Orissa was further separated to become its own distinct province, after which the remaining territory continued simply as the Province of Bihar — a second, independently significant date frequently tested alongside 1912.
Patna's status as a provincial and later state capital dates from this early 20th-century reorganization, cementing its role as Bihar's administrative centre.

The Champaran Satyagraha addressed the grievances of indigo cultivators forced, under the exploitative 'Tinkathia' system, to grow indigo on a fixed proportion (three-twentieths, or roughly 15%) of their landholding for European planters, regardless of market conditions or their own economic interest.

Mahatma Gandhi's intervention in Champaran in 1917, at the invitation of local peasant leader Raj Kumar Shukla, is widely regarded as Gandhi's first major Satyagraha (civil disobedience) campaign within India, following his earlier activism in South Africa.

Rajendra Prasad, who would go on to become independent India's first President, was among the prominent figures who supported Gandhi's efforts during the Champaran movement, marking an early milestone in his own political career.

The movement's success in securing relief for the cultivators and abolishing the Tinkathia system established Satyagraha as a viable and powerful method of political mobilization, subsequently applied by Gandhi in numerous later campaigns across India.
Bihar saw significant participation in the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22) and the Civil Disobedience Movement (1930s), with prominent local leaders mobilizing widespread popular support.

During the Quit India Movement of 1942, Patna witnessed a notably significant episode when student protesters attempting to hoist the national flag at the Secretariat were fired upon, resulting in several deaths — commemorated today by the Shaheed Smarak (Martyrs' Memorial) near the Bihar Vidhan Sabha.

Numerous Bihar-origin leaders played prominent roles at the national level in the freedom movement and subsequent nation-building, a theme explored further in this book's chapter on important personalities.

blocks.content: Table 4.1 — Key Dates in Bihar's Administrative and Political History

cells: Suri Empire under Sher Shah Suri (briefly interrupting Mughal rule)
Bihar and Orissa separated from the Bengal Presidency to form a new province
Champaran Satyagraha — Gandhi's first Satyagraha campaign in India
Orissa separated from Bihar and Orissa Province; Bihar becomes a distinct province
Quit India Movement; Patna Secretariat firing incident
Jharkhand carved out of southern Bihar as a separate state

Exam Tip

• 1912 (Bihar-Orissa separated from Bengal) vs 1936 (Orissa separated from Bihar) is one of the most commonly confused date pairs in Bihar history — always double-check which specific separation a question is asking about.

• The Champaran Satyagraha's specific grievance (the Tinkathia system forcing indigo cultivation on ~15% of land) and its status as Gandhi's first Indian Satyagraha are both frequently and precisely tested facts.

• Sher Shah Suri's administrative legacy (revenue settlement, currency, Grand Trunk Road) is often tested as a set — be ready to identify which specific reform a question is referencing.
